vulnerabilities.name: Unattended agent in CI with permission checks turned off
vulnerabilities.description:
A CI agent with no approvals and the job's token can be steered by anyone who can write an issue, PR, commit message or file it reads, and then push code, read secrets or publish packages.

Found: --dangerously-skip-permissions
vulnerabilities.solution: Keep approvals on, give the job read-only permissions, and run untrusted-input jobs without repository secrets.

identifiers.name: AP02: Unattended agent in CI with permission checks turned off

vulnerabilities.name: Agent workflow triggered by pull_request_target
vulnerabilities.description:
pull_request_target runs with the base repository's secrets and write token on events from forks. An agent that reads the fork's PR text or code can be told to leak or misuse them.

Found: pull_request_target + agent step
vulnerabilities.solution: Use pull_request for agent jobs, or split the job so the agent never sees secrets or a write token while it reads outside content.

identifiers.name: AP03: Agent workflow triggered by pull_request_target

vulnerabilities.name: Agent runs with all permission checks turned off
vulnerabilities.description:
Every tool call, including shell commands and file deletes, runs without approval. One prompt injection in a file, issue or web page the agent reads can run any command as you.

Found: defaultMode: bypassPermissions
vulnerabilities.solution: Remove the bypass. Allow specific tools instead, and run unattended agents in a throwaway sandbox with no secrets and no network beyond what the task needs.

identifiers.name: AP01: Agent runs with all permission checks turned off

vulnerabilities.name: MCP server installed from an unpinned package
vulnerabilities.description:
npx/uvx/bunx fetch the newest version at every start. A hijacked or malicious update becomes code running with your agent's access, with no review.

Found: fs: pnpx fs-mcp@latest
vulnerabilities.solution: Pin an exact version (for example pkg@1.4.2), or install it once from a reviewed lockfile.

identifiers.name: AP04: MCP server installed from an unpinned package
CWE-829

vulnerabilities.name: Secret written directly in agent configuration
vulnerabilities.description:
Config files get committed, copied and read by the agent itself. A literal token is long-lived, shared and easy to leak through the agent's output.

Found: env.API_KEY = <redacted>
vulnerabilities.solution: Load the secret from the environment or a secret manager, use a short-lived scoped token, and rotate the exposed one.

identifiers.name: AP05: Secret written directly in agent configuration
CWE-798

vulnerabilities.name: Agent allowed to run any shell command
vulnerabilities.description:
An allow-rule like Bash(*) or a bare Bash lets the agent run any command without asking. That includes curl to send your files out, rm -rf and git push --force.

Found: allow "Bash(*)"
vulnerabilities.solution: Allow only the specific commands the task needs, such as Bash(npm test), and keep deny rules for network and destructive commands.

identifiers.name: AP06: Agent allowed to run any shell command

vulnerabilities.name: Agent tool container can take over the host
vulnerabilities.description:
--privileged, a mounted Docker socket, host networking or a mounted root filesystem remove the container boundary. A compromised tool then controls the machine.

Found: box: --privileged
vulnerabilities.solution: Drop these flags. Mount only the folders the tool needs, read-only where possible.

identifiers.name: AP08: Agent tool container can take over the host
CWE-250

vulnerabilities.name: Agent workflow anyone can trigger with a comment or issue
vulnerabilities.description:
issue_comment, issues, discussion_comment, pull_request_review_comment and workflow_run run with the repository's secrets and token. Without a check on who triggered it, any GitHub user can write the text the agent reads and steer it.

Found: issue_comment + agent step, no actor check
vulnerabilities.solution: Gate the job on the actor: an if: on author_association (OWNER, MEMBER, COLLABORATOR) or a permission check, keep the vendor actions' write-access check on, and give the job read-only permissions.

identifiers.name: AP21: Agent workflow anyone can trigger with a comment or issue

vulnerabilities.name: Hidden Unicode characters in agent instructions
vulnerabilities.description:
Bidirectional controls, zero-width characters and Unicode tag characters are invisible in review but read by the model. A rules file or tool description can carry instructions no reviewer saw.

Found: 3 hidden character(s) on 1 line(s): U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE, U+E0049 TAG, U+E0047 TAG
vulnerabilities.solution: Remove the characters (the finding names each code point), and block them in review or CI for agent instruction files and tool descriptions.

identifiers.name: AP22: Hidden Unicode characters in agent instructions

vulnerabilities.name: Hook or skill runs code fetched from the internet
vulnerabilities.description:
A hook or skill that pipes a download into a shell (curl ... | sh) runs whatever that URL serves today, on every machine that uses the setting, with the agent's and the user's access.

Found: hook runs curl -fsSL https://hooks.example.org/h.sh | sh
vulnerabilities.solution: Vendor the script into the repository, or download a pinned version and check its hash before running it.

identifiers.name: AP23: Hook or skill runs code fetched from the internet
CWE-494

vulnerabilities.name: Remote MCP server reached over plain HTTP
vulnerabilities.description:
Tool calls, results and credentials cross the network unencrypted and can be read or changed in transit, including the tool descriptions the model trusts.

Found: remote: http://tools.example.org
vulnerabilities.solution: Use https, and authenticate the server.

identifiers.name: AP07: Remote MCP server reached over plain HTTP
CWE-319

vulnerabilities.name: Lethal combination: untrusted input, private data and a way out
vulnerabilities.description:
The same agent can read content an attacker controls, reach private data and send data or act outside. Prompt injection then becomes data theft; no system prompt reliably stops it.

Found: likely, from server and package names — untrusted input: gmail; private data: gmail, postgres; a way out: gmail
vulnerabilities.solution: Split the capabilities across agents, remove one leg, or require a person to approve every outbound or consequential action.

identifiers.name: AP09: Lethal combination: untrusted input, private data and a way out

vulnerabilities.name: Agent tools approved automatically, without review
vulnerabilities.description:
Settings such as enableAllProjectMcpServers, an MCP server's alwaysAllow or autoApprove list, Gemini CLI's trust: true or VS Code's chat.tools.autoApprove start servers or run tool calls without asking. Injected text, or a project file someone else wrote, then acts with no person in the loop.

Found: enableAllProjectMcpServers: true (project MCP servers start without approval)
vulnerabilities.solution: Approve servers one at a time and leave tool calls on ask. Auto-approve only read-only tools you have reviewed, and never in settings committed to a shared repository.

identifiers.name: AP20: Agent tools approved automatically, without review

vulnerabilities.name: Agent image not pinned to a digest
vulnerabilities.description:
A mutable tag such as :latest can change under you, so what you tested is not what runs.

Found: FROM node:20
vulnerabilities.solution: Pin the base image by digest (image@sha256:...) and update it on purpose.

identifiers.name: AP10: Agent image not pinned to a digest
CWE-829
